Pluto doesn't meet the criteria that make the eight planets a distinct class. Under the International Astronomical Union's 2006 definition, a planet must orbit the Sun, be massive enough to pull itself into a round shape, and have cleared its orbital neighborhood of other debris. Pluto passes the first two tests but fails the third. It's one of many icy bodies in the Kuiper Belt, and its mass is only a tiny fraction of everything else sharing its region.

The reclassification also reflects real discovery. Once astronomers found Eris, which is roughly Pluto's size, and a growing list of similar objects (Makemake, Haumea, and others), the choice was either to admit dozens of new "planets" or to recognize Pluto as part of a different population. On this view, the extinction resulted from long-term volcanic forcing, with Chicxulub delivering the coup de grâce rather than doing most of the killing.
